metric.primary: recall@5 -- does expected_any appear in the top 5 results
configurations: 3. FTS over identifiers + localized names + descriptions
4. plus embeddings, only if 2-3 prove insufficient
$comment: Report per tier, never as a single aggregate. An aggregate hides the whole
point: tier lexical-id passes under every configuration and would mask a

tiers.lexical-id: Query words appear in the identifier. Config 1 should already pass. Control group -- if these fail, the index is broken, not the design.
tiers.lexical-name: Query words appear ONLY in the localized display name. Config 1 must fail and config 2 must pass. THIS TIER IS THE DECISION POINT for whether localization indexing earns its place. Cases marked "overlap": "partial" share a token with the identifier and are therefore weaker evidence -- config 1 can reach the right family by that token alone. Score the 12 clean cases separately from the 3 partial ones; the clean subset is what the decision rests on.
tiers.lexical-description: Query words appear only in the description. Separates indexing names from indexing descriptions -- only 305 items have descriptions, so this tier is small by nature.
tiers.semantic: No literal overlap with identifier, name or description. Expected to fail configs 1-3. Measures the headroom embeddings would buy; do NOT treat failures here as bugs.
tiers.disambiguation: The phrase is genuinely ambiguous. Correct behaviour is surfacing both senses, not picking one. Scored as: are both senses present in the top 5.
tiers.noise-rejection: Vanilla ships 180 Prototype_, 28 Debug_, 17 Template_, 13 Filter_ and 6 Test_ items. A real asset must outrank them. Scored as: is the top result a non-noise asset.
tiers.locale-cyrillic: Nominative-form queries in Ukrainian and Russian. Baseline proof that non-Latin locales are indexed at all. Should pass with plain FTS once every locale is indexed and text is normalised.
tiers.locale-cjk: Chinese. Two distinct problems: whole-word queries, and INFIX queries where the meaningful noun sits at the END of a compound (蜘蛛 'spider' inside 洞穴蜘蛛 'cave spider'). unicode61 treats an ideograph run as one token, so infix works only because normalizeSearchText() segments ideographs. Prefix indexing alone cannot reach these.
tiers.inflection: Full inflected Ukrainian and Russian forms, as a user would actually type them. SQLite ships no Cyrillic stemmer, and FTS5 prefix matching needs the QUERY to be a prefix of the INDEXED term -- so 'кірасу' misses 'кіраса', which diverges at the last letter. These pass only via progressive suffix trimming (buildRelaxedMatchExpressions). An English-only eval set cannot see any of this.
tiers.orthography: Characters users type differently from how the corpus spells them. Ukrainian Ґ (U+0490) is a distinct letter, not a diacritic, so remove_diacritics does not fold it -- yet Ukrainians routinely type plain г.
tiers.cross-locale: The same asset reached through several languages. A creator working in Ukrainian may still search an English name seen in a tutorial, so search must cover every indexed locale regardless of the display language.

cases.why: The identifier says Armory. Nothing in the identifier space contains 'forge'.
Identifier is Bench_Weapon -- neither word appears in it.

The canonical example from 03-ARCHITECTURE.md: identifier says Chest, player sees Cuirass. NOTE: 'adamantite' also appears in the identifier, so config 1 can reach the right family and may land it in the top 5 by luck. The discriminating token is 'cuirass' alone. Weaker evidence than the clean cases -- weight accordingly.
Zero token overlap with the identifier.

01-VISION.md uses this phrase as its motivating example, but measurement moved it out of lexical-name: the identifier Spider_Cave contains BOTH query tokens, merely reordered. It tests underscore tokenisation and word-order independence, not localization. Keeping it mislabelled would have made configs 1 and 2 look equivalent -- exactly the trap 09-EVALUATION.md warns about.
Single token in the name, two underscore-separated tokens in the identifier -- tests tokenizer behaviour as much as source.
'Kweebec' is the internal species name; players only ever see 'Rootling'. 'merchant' overlaps the identifier, so config 1 can reach merchants generally -- 'rootling' is the discriminating token.
'dragon' overlaps; 'ember' is the discriminating token. Config 1 will find dragons but cannot tell Fire from the rest.

'Invisible' appears only in the description: 'Invisible Block use to block off areas.' An earlier revision phrased this as 'invisible block to wall off an area' and failed — the description says 'block off', not 'wall off', and every term must match. Long conversational phrasings belong in the semantic tier, where failure is the expected result.
Description opens 'Use to quickly regain health.' The name is just 'Bandage'.

Neither the identifier nor the name contains 'kitchen'; only the description does. Previously phrased '...for advanced dishes', which failed on the word 'for' — the description reads 'can be used to make advanced dishes'.

cases.phrase: used to create potions and elixirs

cases.why: No shared token with identifier, name or description.

cases.phrase: light I can mount on a wall

cases.why: Two unrelated senses: storage furniture, and the chest armor slot. Both must surface; picking one silently is the failure.
Bench_Campfire is named exactly 'Campfire'; Furniture_Crude_Brazier is 'Small Campfire' and Deco_Campfire_Off is 'Dead Embers'. Exact-name match should win, near matches should still appear.
TRAP. The identifier says Legs; the display name says Boots. Any system reasoning from identifiers puts this in the wrong equipment slot. Verified, not a typo on our side.

A FAMILY query -- any real sword counts. The hazard measured here is not test assets but UNLOCALIZED ones: Server/Item/Animations/Sword.json has the cleanest possible identifier match and outranked every weapon until localized rows were ordered first.
The prototype is a decorative sign, not a projectile.
Every match is a Prototype_. Correct behaviour is to return them while marking them as prototypes -- an empty expected_any means we are scoring the labelling, not the recall.
The identifier says Pickaxe; Ukrainian says кайло, which shares nothing with it. The Cyrillic analogue of the forge/Bench_Armory case.
Whole-word CJK. Works even without segmentation; the baseline for this tier.

INFIX. 蜘蛛 ('spider') is the trailing half of 洞穴蜘蛛 ('cave spider'). Prefix indexing cannot reach a trailing substring; only ideograph segmentation can. Measured to return nothing before normalisation was added.
INFIX, and not even aligned to a word boundary -- the query spans characters 2-3 of a three-character name.

cases.display: 精金胸甲 / 钴胸甲 / 铜胸甲 / 铁胸甲 / 钢胸甲
cases.why: INFIX. 胸甲 is 'cuirass' -- the same semantic case as the English tier, in a script where the technique that makes it work is entirely different. A FAMILY query: every chest armor legitimately matches, so expecting one specific material was an error in an earlier revision, not a defect in the index.

Accusative. 'кірасу' is NOT a prefix of 'кіраса' -- they diverge at the final letter -- so prefix matching alone returns nothing. Verified: this is the case that disproved an earlier claim that prefix indexing substitutes for stemming.
Feminine genitive of an adjective: four characters differ from the indexed form. Needs the deepest trim level.
Both words inflect at once -- adjective agreement plus animate accusative.

The corpus spells it with Ґ (U+0490); most users type plain г. These are separate Cyrillic letters, so remove_diacritics does NOT fold them -- normalizeSearchText() does, on both sides. Measured to return nothing without it.

cases.display: Forge / Ковальня / Кузница / Forja / 锻炉
cases.why: Together with the four rows below: one asset must be reachable from every shipped language, whatever the user's display locale. Scored as a group -- all five must resolve to the same asset.
Four letters, so suffix trimming is refused -- proves relaxation does not fire where it would match everything.
